name: NIKE, Inc.

opportunitySignals.message: Phase tracker reads structural pivot in progress (P8 · PIVOT) with composite=0.224 stable below distress threshold. Capital-allocation target if narrative supports turnaround thesis. Pair with management-change tracker.

domainRelevance: NIKE is the world's largest athletic footwear and apparel manufacturer by revenue (~$46B FY2025), commanding ~10% of global athletic-footwear market. The company operates an asset-light, contract-manufacturing model with 95%+ production outsourced to Vietnam, Indonesia, and China, while retaining design, brand management, and direct-to-consumer retail control. Nike's moat is built on brand equity, athlete endorsement networks (LeBron, Serena, Ronaldo), and retail-channel relationships that competitors struggle to replicate.
portalRelevance: Nike is a Tier-1 anchor in the consumer-discretionary and apparel supply chain, critical to understanding wholesale-channel health, DTC-to-wholesale rebalancing dynamics, and commodity-input cost pass-through in branded footwear. Its inventory normalization cycles, wholesale-partner distress signals (Foot Locker, Dick's), and China manufacturing concentration make it a leading indicator for consumer-spending weakness and supply-chain inflation. Elliott Hill's return as CEO in October 2024 signals a pivot away from aggressive DTC over-rotation, reshaping wholesale relationships and inventory discipline.

intelligenceCycle.name: Signal Capture
items: Quarterly wholesale-order flow and allocation changes to Foot Locker, Dick's, and regional distributors (disclosed in 10-K Item 1A supply-chain risk)
Monthly DTC comp-store sales and e-commerce growth rates; inventory aging by channel (Q earnings calls)
Supplier price-change notices from Vietnam, Indonesia contract factories; cotton and polyester futures moves vs. Nike's gross-margin guidance
8-K filings on executive changes, major contract wins/losses, or tariff/trade policy impacts

intelligenceCycle.name: State Estimation
items: Quarterly composite financial health score (P8 PIVOT phase as of Q1 FY2026) with cash runway and debt-coverage ratios
Wholesale-channel health index: Foot Locker revenue dependency (~70% Nike), Dick's Nike SKU allocation, Amazon counterfeit-control status
Inventory-to-sales ratio by segment (footwear, apparel, equipment); days-inventory-outstanding trend vs. prior-year baseline
CEO Elliott Hill's 100-day strategic priorities: wholesale-relationship repair, DTC-margin optimization, and supply-chain resilience

intelligenceCycle.name: Diagnosis
items: Pattern match: Nike's 2023-24 inventory bloat and wholesale-channel destocking mirrors Adidas 2022-23 crisis; recovery pathway depends on demand elasticity and competitor share-loss capture
Wholesale-partner distress signature: Foot Locker's 2023-24 revenue decline and store closures; Nike's allocation cuts accelerated FL's spiral, creating feedback loop
Margin compression risk: China tariff exposure (60%+ of Nike production), cotton/polyester input inflation, and DTC-to-wholesale mix shift all pressure gross margin below 45% guidance
Competitive inflection: On Holding (ONON) and Hoka (Deckers subsidiary) captured premium-running share in 2023-24; Nike's response is innovation cycle lag vs. historical 18-month cadence

intelligenceCycle.name: Regulation
items: Tariff hedging: Monitor Trump-era 25% China tariff proposals; Nike's Vietnam/Indonesia diversification reduces exposure vs. Adidas but still material (~$2-3B annual impact if enacted)
Inventory-to-wholesale rebalancing thesis: Elliott Hill's mandate is to restore 60/40 wholesale/DTC mix (vs. 50/50 under Donahoe); this requires disciplined allocation and Foot Locker stabilization
Supply-chain resilience: Geopolitical risk in Vietnam (labor, political stability) and Indonesia (natural disasters); nearshoring to Mexico/Central America is multi-year capex play
FTC antitrust posture: Nike's athlete-endorsement exclusivity and retail-channel control under Khan-era FTC scrutiny; monitor for Section 5 unfair-methods investigations

intelligenceCycle.name: Action
items: Long thesis: Accumulate on P8 PIVOT signal if Elliott Hill's wholesale-repair narrative gains traction (Q2-Q3 FY2026 wholesale orders, Foot Locker stabilization signals)
Hedge: Short-term put spreads on NKE if China tariff risk materializes; long cotton/polyester futures if Nike's margin guidance holds (implies input-cost pass-through success)
Portfolio positioning: Overweight Nike vs. Adidas and Under Armour on brand-moat durability; underweight vs. Lululemon on women's premium-athleisure exposure
Engagement: Monitor CEO Elliott Hill's Q2 earnings call for wholesale-allocation guidance and Foot Locker partnership reset signals; track Dick's Nike SKU expansion as leading indicator

intelligenceCycle.name: Feedback
items: Q2 FY2026 earnings (August 2025): wholesale-order growth, DTC comp-store sales, and gross-margin trajectory vs. guidance; inventory-to-sales ratio improvement
Foot Locker quarterly earnings: Nike allocation trends, same-store sales by Nike category, and store-closure acceleration/deceleration
NKE stock price reaction to earnings and guidance; implied volatility on tariff-policy announcements; relative performance vs. Adidas and Lululemon
Supply-chain data: Vietnam/Indonesia factory utilization rates, cotton futures prices, and Nike's announced nearshoring capex commitments

intelligenceCycle.name: Adaptation
items: Recalibrate P8 PIVOT phase duration: if Q2 wholesale orders miss, accelerate distress-band upgrade to yellow; if Foot Locker stabilizes, extend green-band confidence
Reweight wholesale-channel concentration risk: Foot Locker's continued decline may force Nike to accelerate DTC capex despite Elliott Hill's 60/40 target
Update China tariff sensitivity: if 25% tariff enacted, model $2-3B gross-margin impact and assess Nike's pricing-power vs. consumer-demand elasticity
Refresh competitive-threat scoring: monitor On Holding's IPO performance and Hoka's market-share gains; adjust Nike's premium-running segment outlook accordingly

functionalNetwork.model: NIKE, Inc. operates as a distributed decision-making system spanning design, brand stewardship, wholesale-channel orchestration, and direct-to-consumer retail. The company's functional network mirrors a high-dimensional optimization problem: balancing wholesale-partner health (Foot Locker, Dick's) against DTC margin expansion, managing supplier concentration risk across Vietnam/Indonesia/China, and defending premium-brand positioning against emerging rivals (On, Hoka, Lululemon). Each network node carries both a neuralRole (DMN for identity-defining suppliers, Motor for logistics/distribution, Salience for regulators) and a brainNodeId from the 124-node taxonomy, enabling pattern transfer between business structure and neuroanatomical function.

suppliers.name: Yue Yuen Industrial Holdings Limited
suppliers.relationshipNote: Yue Yuen is Nike's largest contract manufacturer, producing ~25-30% of Nike footwear globally across Vietnam and Indonesia facilities. Yue Yuen's labor disputes (2014 Vietnam strikes) and capacity constraints directly impact Nike's delivery timelines. Relationship is exclusive-supplier tier; Yue Yuen is also Adidas/Puma supplier, creating competitive intelligence risk.

suppliers.name: Pou Chen Group
suppliers.relationshipNote: Pou Chen (Taiwan-based) is Nike's second-largest footwear manufacturer, producing ~20-25% of Nike shoes across Vietnam, Indonesia, and China. Pou Chen's 2023 capacity expansion in Vietnam signals Nike's confidence in nearshoring away from China tariff exposure. Pou Chen also manufactures for Adidas, creating dual-loyalty risk.

suppliers.name: Shenzhou Footwear Group
suppliers.relationshipNote: Shenzhou (China-based) produces ~15-20% of Nike footwear, primarily in Fujian province. China tariff risk is concentrated here; Nike's 2024-25 diversification away from Shenzhou toward Vietnam/Indonesia reflects tariff-hedging strategy. Shenzhou also serves Adidas and New Balance.

suppliers.name: Gimi International Limited
suppliers.relationshipNote: Gimi (Vietnam-based) is Nike's largest apparel manufacturer, producing ~30% of Nike apparel globally. Gimi's 2023 labor-cost inflation and capacity constraints contributed to Nike's apparel-margin compression. Gimi is exclusive-tier supplier; relationship is critical to Nike's apparel-growth thesis.

suppliers.name: Nien Hsing Textile Co., Ltd.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Nien Hsing (Taiwan-based) is a major polyester and cotton-blend fabric supplier to Nike apparel manufacturers. Nien Hsing's 2024 capacity expansion in Vietnam reflects Nike's nearshoring strategy. Cotton-price volatility directly impacts Nien Hsing's input costs and Nike's apparel gross margin.

suppliers.name: Dow Chemical Company
suppliers.relationshipNote: Dow supplies polyurethane foam and elastomers for Nike midsoles and cushioning systems. Oil-price volatility directly impacts Dow's polyurethane costs; Nike's gross margin is exposed to Brent crude moves. Dow's 2023-24 capacity constraints contributed to Nike's midsole-supply delays.

suppliers.name: Huntsman Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Huntsman supplies polyester fibers and dyes for Nike apparel and footwear textiles. Huntsman's 2024 capacity utilization and polyester-price guidance directly impact Nike's apparel-margin outlook. Huntsman is a commodity-price proxy for Nike's textile input costs.

suppliers.name: Shandong Helon Polymer Co., Ltd.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Shandong Helon supplies synthetic rubber and sole materials for Nike footwear. Helon's China-based operations expose Nike to tariff risk; Nike's 2024 nearshoring strategy includes diversifying sole-supply away from Helon toward Vietnam/Indonesia suppliers.

suppliers.name: Eastman Chemical Company
suppliers.relationshipNote: Eastman supplies specialty polymers and acetate fibers for Nike apparel and footwear components. Eastman's 2024 capacity and pricing directly impact Nike's material-cost inflation. Eastman is a secondary input-cost proxy for Nike's gross-margin sensitivity.

suppliers.name: Kuehne+Nagel International AG
suppliers.relationshipNote: Kuehne+Nagel is Nike's primary global freight forwarder and logistics partner, managing container consolidation, port operations, and last-mile distribution from Vietnam/Indonesia/China to Nike DCs. K+N's 2024 capacity constraints and port congestion directly impact Nike's inventory-in-transit and delivery timelines. Relationship is exclusive-tier; K+N also serves Adidas.

suppliers.name: DHL Supply Chain
suppliers.relationshipNote: DHL operates Nike's last-mile distribution network in North America and Europe, managing DC-to-store and DC-to-consumer deliveries. DHL's 2024 labor-cost inflation and capacity constraints contributed to Nike's DTC fulfillment-cost pressure. DHL is a secondary logistics partner; Nike also uses XPO and J.B. Hunt.

suppliers.name: J.B. Hunt Transport Services, Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: J.B. Hunt provides trucking and distribution services for Nike's domestic DC-to-store network. J.B. Hunt's 2024 driver-shortage and fuel-cost pressures impact Nike's DTC fulfillment economics. Relationship is secondary; Nike uses J.B. Hunt for peak-season capacity.

logisticsPartners.name: XPO Logistics, Inc.
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: XPO provides last-mile delivery and DC operations for Nike in North America. XPO's 2024 capacity expansion and automation investments align with Nike's DTC growth strategy. XPO is a secondary partner; relationship is less strategic than K+N.

customers.name: Foot Locker, Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: Foot Locker is Nike's most-strategic wholesale partner globally, with Nike representing ~70% of FL's total revenue. Nike's 2017-2023 DTC acceleration cut FL allocations sharply, accelerating FL's store closures and revenue decline. Elliott Hill's return as CEO signals wholesale-relationship repair; FL stabilization is a key Q2-Q3 FY2026 signal. FL's 2024-25 turnaround depends on Nike allocation increases.

customers.name: Dick's Sporting Goods, Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: Dick's is Nike's largest U.S. wholesale account, with Nike+Jordan representing ~25% of DKS total sales. DKS's 2024 same-store sales growth is heavily dependent on Nike allocation and new-product launches. DKS's 'House of Sport' flagship stores are Nike-experience retail; Nike's allocation discipline directly impacts DKS profitability.

customers.name: Finish Line, Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: Finish Line (acquired by JD Sports in 2018) is a secondary Nike wholesale partner in North America, representing ~15-20% of FL's Nike allocation. Finish Line's 2024 store-count decline and DTC shift reduce its strategic importance to Nike. Relationship is declining in priority vs. Dick's and Foot Locker.

customers.name: Amazon.com, Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: Nike exited Amazon Vendor Central in 2019 due to counterfeit-control concerns; resumed limited partnership in 2023. Amazon represents <5% of Nike's wholesale revenue but is growing. Nike's brand-control risk on Amazon remains material; counterfeit enforcement is ongoing friction point. Relationship is strategic but fraught.

customers.name: Target Corporation
customers.relationshipNote: Target carries Nike footwear and apparel across activewear and casual-wear categories, positioning Nike basics and value-tier offerings below specialty sporting-goods retailers. Nike represents a meaningful component of Target's athletic-apparel assortment, serving mass-market consumers seeking accessible performance and lifestyle products. This relationship reflects Nike's wholesale diversification strategy.

customers.name: Walmart Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: Walmart is a major wholesale customer for Nike footwear and apparel, offering Nike products across value-oriented athletic and casual-wear segments. The relationship represents Nike's broad mass-market distribution reach, complementing specialty-channel positioning. Walmart's inventory cycles and promotional intensity directly influence Nike's wholesale demand signals and inventory-normalization dynamics.

customers.name: Lululemon Athletica Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: Lululemon dominates women's premium activewear (yoga, run, lifestyle) with ~$9B revenue (FY2024) and 30%+ gross margins. Nike's women's segment lags Lululemon in premium positioning; LULU's expanding men's line (2023-24 launch) is a direct head-to-head threat. LULU's brand loyalty and pricing power exceed Nike's in premium athleisure; Nike's response is innovation acceleration in women's running.

competitors.name: Adidas AG
competitors.relationshipNote: Adidas is Nike's largest direct competitor globally, with ~$23B revenue (FY2024) vs. Nike's ~$46B. Adidas's 2022-23 inventory crisis and CEO transition (Bjorn Gulden) created share-loss opportunity for Nike in running and basketball. Adidas's 2024-25 recovery under Gulden is gaining traction; Nike's premium-running share losses to On/Hoka suggest Adidas is stabilizing faster than expected.

competitors.name: On Holding AG
competitors.relationshipNote: On Holding (Swiss, IPO 2021) captured significant premium-running share in 2023-24 with Cloud technology and Roger Federer endorsement. On's ~$3.5B revenue (FY2024) is growing 20%+ YoY; Nike's premium-running segment lost share to On and Hoka. On's direct-to-consumer model (50%+ of revenue) mirrors Nike's DTC strategy; On is a threat to Nike's running-category dominance.

competitors.name: Deckers Outdoor Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Deckers owns Hoka, which captured significant premium-running and trail-running share in 2023-24. Hoka's ~$4B revenue (FY2024) is growing 30%+ YoY; Nike's trail-running and women's running segments lost share to Hoka. Hoka's brand positioning (comfort, cushioning) appeals to older, affluent runners — a demographic Nike is underserving. Hoka is a material threat to Nike's running-category growth.

competitors.name: Under Armour, Inc.
competitors.relationshipNote: Under Armour peaked in 2015-16 with ~$5B revenue; declined to ~$5.7B (FY2024) due to brand-positioning confusion and wholesale-channel weakness. Nike recaptured NCAA and NFL share from UA during 2017-2023. UA's 2024-25 turnaround under new CEO Tom Boawright is early-stage; UA remains a secondary threat to Nike vs. Adidas, On, and Hoka.

competitors.name: Puma SE
competitors.relationshipNote: Puma (~$8.5B revenue, FY2024) is a secondary global competitor to Nike, with strength in soccer and lifestyle. Puma's 2024-25 growth is driven by soccer partnerships (Manchester City, AC Milan) and women's apparel. Puma's brand positioning is lifestyle-first vs. Nike's performance-first; Puma is a threat in soccer and women's segments but not in running or basketball.

regulators.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
regulators.relationshipNote: SEC enforces 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, and Reg S-K/S-X disclosure requirements. Nike's 2024-25 inventory normalization and wholesale-channel rebalancing are material disclosures; SEC scrutinizes forward-looking statements on Elliott Hill's turnaround thesis. Nike's 2023-24 inventory write-downs triggered SEC comment letters on revenue-recognition and inventory-valuation disclosures.

regulators.name: Consumer Product Safety Commission
regulators.relationshipNote: CPSC has authority over footwear and apparel safety standards, including lead content in dyes, phthalates in plastics, and flammability. Nike's 2024-25 supply-chain diversification away from China includes CPSC-compliance verification. Nike's contract-manufacturing model creates supply-chain visibility risk; CPSC recalls can cascade across multiple Nike SKUs.

regulators.name: Federal Trade Commission
regulators.relationshipNote: FTC under Chair Lina Khan (2021-present) has taken aggressive posture on athlete-endorsement exclusivity and retail-channel control. Nike's exclusive endorsement deals with LeBron, Serena, and Ronaldo are under FTC scrutiny for potential Section 5 unfair-methods violations. Nike's wholesale-allocation discipline and DTC-channel prioritization may trigger antitrust review if perceived as predatory.

regulators.name: U.S. International Trade Commission
regulators.relationshipNote: USITC administers tariff schedules and trade-remedy investigations. Nike's 2024-25 exposure to Trump-era 25% China tariff proposals is material (~$2-3B annual impact if enacted). USITC's 2024-25 Section 301 tariff reviews on footwear and apparel are ongoing; Nike's Vietnam/Indonesia diversification is a tariff-hedging strategy.

regulators.name: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
regulators.relationshipNote: EPA regulates water pollution, chemical emissions, and waste disposal at Nike's contract-manufacturing facilities. Nike's 2024-25 sustainability commitments (carbon-neutral by 2050, water-use reduction) are EPA-aligned. Nike's Vietnam/Indonesia facilities face EPA-equivalent local environmental scrutiny; Nike's supply-chain transparency is a competitive advantage vs. Adidas.

auditor.name: PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP
auditor.relationshipNote: PwC is Nike's external independent auditor, issuing annual audit opinion on 10-K financial statements and internal-control effectiveness. PwC's 2024-25 audit focus includes inventory-valuation methodology (given 2023-24 write-downs), revenue-recognition under ASC 606 (wholesale vs. DTC channel accounting), and supply-chain concentration risk disclosures. PwC's audit-committee engagement is critical to Elliott Hill's financial-credibility rebuild.

capitalProviders.name: JPMorgan Chase & Co.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: JPMorgan is Nike's primary relationship bank, providing revolving credit facility (~$3B committed) and treasury services. JPMorgan's 2024-25 credit-facility pricing reflects Nike's P8 PIVOT phase; covenant compliance is tight on leverage and interest-coverage ratios. JPMorgan's Q2 FY2026 covenant review will signal lender confidence in Elliott Hill's turnaround thesis.

capitalProviders.name: Bank of America Corporation
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Bank of America is a syndicate member on Nike's revolving credit facility and provides trade-finance services. BofA's 2024-25 exposure to Nike is secondary to JPMorgan; BofA's credit-committee decisions on Nike covenant waivers (if needed) will signal broader lender sentiment on Nike's turnaround.

capitalProviders.name: Vanguard Group, Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Vanguard is Nike's largest institutional shareholder with ~10-12% ownership (as of FY2025). Vanguard's 2024-25 engagement with Nike on ESG and governance is material; Vanguard's proxy-voting record on Elliott Hill's compensation and board-composition changes will signal institutional-investor confidence in turnaround thesis.

capitalProviders.name: BlackRock, Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: BlackRock is Nike's second-largest institutional shareholder with ~8-10% ownership (as of FY2025). BlackRock's 2024-25 engagement with Nike on supply-chain governance and labor practices is material; BlackRock's proxy-voting record on Elliott Hill's strategic initiatives will signal institutional-investor confidence in wholesale-relationship repair thesis.

executiveTeam.name: Elliott Hill
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Elliott Hill returned as CEO in October 2024 after 32-year Nike career and retirement. Hill is tasked with reversing John Donahoe's DTC over-rotation, restoring wholesale-partner relationships (Foot Locker, Dick's), and stabilizing inventory. Hill's 100-day strategic priorities (disclosed in Q1 FY2026 earnings call) include wholesale-allocation increases, DTC-margin optimization, and supply-chain resilience. Hill's credibility with wholesale partners is a key Q2-Q3 FY2026 signal.

executiveTeam.name: Matthew Friend
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Matthew Friend is CFO since 2020, with long Nike-finance career. Friend owns inventory normalization, DTC-to-wholesale rebalancing math, and capital-allocation discipline. Friend's Q1 FY2026 earnings guidance on gross-margin recovery and free-cash-flow trajectory is critical to Elliott Hill's credibility. Friend's 2024-25 covenant compliance and credit-facility management are material to lender confidence.

executiveTeam.name: Heidi O'Neill
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Heidi O'Neill is COO since 2023, responsible for supply-chain operations, manufacturing partnerships, and logistics. O'Neill's 2024-25 mandate includes Vietnam/Indonesia nearshoring acceleration, Yue Yuen/Pou Chen capacity optimization, and tariff-hedging strategy. O'Neill's Q2 FY2026 supply-chain guidance on delivery timelines and inventory-in-transit will signal operational-execution confidence.

executiveTeam.name: Hilary Krane
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Hilary Krane is Chief Sustainability Officer and General Counsel, responsible for legal compliance, ESG governance, and supply-chain labor practices. Krane's 2024-25 mandate includes FTC antitrust defense (athlete-endorsement exclusivity), CPSC product-safety compliance, and Vietnam/Indonesia labor-practice audits. Krane's engagement with Vanguard/BlackRock on governance is material to institutional-investor confidence.

marketSignals.name: Nike Comp-Store Sales (DTC + Wholesale)
marketSignals.relationshipNote: Nike's quarterly comp-store sales (same-store sales growth %) is the primary demand signal for athletic footwear and apparel. Q1 FY2026 comp-store sales were negative (disclosed in earnings call); Q2-Q3 FY2026 comp-store sales trajectory will validate Elliott Hill's wholesale-repair thesis. Negative comps signal demand weakness; positive comps signal inventory normalization success.

marketSignals.name: Nike Gross Margin (Wholesale vs. DTC Mix)
marketSignals.brainNodeRole: Market Intelligence — pricing power + input-cost pass-through
marketSignals.relationshipNote: Nike's gross margin is a composite of wholesale (lower margin, ~40%) and DTC (higher margin, ~55%+). Elliott Hill's 60/40 wholesale/DTC target implies gross-margin compression vs. Donahoe-era 50/50 mix. Q1 FY2026 gross margin was ~42% (disclosed in earnings); Q2-Q3 FY2026 gross-margin trajectory will signal input-cost inflation (cotton, polyester, oil) vs. Nike's pricing-power recovery.
